source_refs.note: Topic 21.3.2 (PDF 81-82); the E2 and E1 schemes are redrawn. The book's E1 carbocation is drawn with a CH2 group; it is (CH3)3C+.

blocks.text: Beta-elimination is a reaction in which a hydrogen atom on the beta carbon (the carbon next to the one carrying the halogen) and the halogen atom are removed. It happens when a base attacks the beta hydrogen; the halogen leaves at the same time or afterwards, and an alkene forms instead of a substitution product. Elimination takes place alongside substitution and often competes with it. Like substitution, it can follow two mechanisms, E2 or E1.

items: E2 (bimolecular): the base attacks the beta hydrogen and the leaving group departs at the same time as the C=C double bond forms, in one step. The rate depends on both the halogenoalkane and the base: rate = k[halogenoalkane][base], second order.

E1 (unimolecular): like SN1, the first step is the slow ionisation of the substrate to a carbocation; in the second step the base removes a beta hydrogen to give the alkene. The rate depends only on the halogenoalkane: rate = k[halogenoalkane].

blocks.alt: Top, E2: a base B- attacks a hydrogen on the CH3 carbon of bromoethane, the C-H electrons move into the C-C bond and the C-Br electrons move onto Br, all at once, giving CH2=CH2 + H-B + Br-. Bottom, E1: (CH3)3C-Br ionises slowly to (CH3)3C+ + Br-; then a base removes a hydrogen from a methyl group, giving 2-methylpropene (CH3)2C=CH2.
blocks.caption: The E2 and E1 mechanisms (original diagram after the book's schemes).
blocks.long_description: In E2 everything happens in one concerted step: the base takes the beta hydrogen, the new pi bond forms and the bromide leaves. In E1 the carbocation forms first, exactly as in SN1, and only then does the base take a proton from the neighbouring carbon to form the double bond.

blocks.text: Primary halogenoalkanes generally follow E2 and tertiary halogenoalkanes E1, while secondary halogenoalkanes can show either, depending on the solvent.

blocks.explanation: No: the beta carbon, C(CH3)3, carries no hydrogen, so there is no beta hydrogen for a base to remove.

items: Beta-elimination removes a beta-H and X to give an alkene.
E2: one step, rate = k[RX][base]; E1: via a carbocation, rate = k[RX].
Primary: E2; tertiary: E1; secondary: either.
